candidates.speaker: Andrew Loke
candidates.proposition: A causal series must have a first cause if it has neither an infinite regress nor a closed causal loop.
candidates.attributionBasis: The host explicitly hands the presentation to Loke, who continuously presents the numbered reformulated argument throughout this window.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This deduction supplies the first-cause stage on which every later inference to a beginningless personal creator depends.
candidates.contextSummary: Loke introduces a causal series, exhausts the alternatives as infinite regress, closed loop, or first cause, and states that excluding the first two yields the third.

candidates.speaker: Andrew Loke
candidates.proposition: The first cause is beginningless and initially changeless because whatever begins has a cause and every change is a beginning event.
candidates.attributionBasis: Loke remains the uninterrupted presenter and explicitly develops consequences of the first cause established in his preceding premises.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The move derives two defining properties needed to distinguish the proposed first cause from the Big Bang and other beginning events.
candidates.contextSummary: Loke invokes the causal principle, defines changes as events with beginnings, excludes an event such as the Big Bang from being first, and concludes initial changelessness.

candidates.speaker: Andrew Loke
candidates.proposition: An initially changeless first cause must be transcendent and immaterial rather than a constantly changing material or quantum system.
candidates.attributionBasis: The uninterrupted first-person presentation continues, with Loke deriving additional properties of his expressly identified first cause.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This inference advances the argument from a generic first cause toward the nonphysical creator described by the debate motion.
candidates.contextSummary: Loke characterizes transcendence as beyond ordinary experience and argues that material and quantum systems constantly change, unlike the initially changeless first cause.

candidates.speaker: Andrew Loke
candidates.proposition: Originating an event without prior determination while retaining the capacity not to change requires libertarian freedom and therefore personal agency.
candidates.attributionBasis: Loke remains the sole presenter and explicitly reasons from the first cause's two capacities to freedom, agency, and personhood.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This is the principal bridge from an initially changeless first cause to the personal creator asserted in the motion.
candidates.contextSummary: Loke says the first cause must initiate an event by itself yet be able to remain changeless; he identifies this dual capacity as libertarian freedom implying an agent.

candidates.speaker: Andrew Loke
candidates.proposition: Several independent arguments can exclude an infinite causal regress, so defending even one successful argument is sufficient for the first-cause case.
candidates.attributionBasis: Loke continues his announced presentation, enumerating regress arguments from his book and specifying which one he intends to defend.
candidates.loadBearingReason: Excluding infinite regress is one of Loke's identified crucial premises, and this move states his cumulative and independent defense strategy.
candidates.contextSummary: Loke lists Hilbert's Hotel, traversal, dependence-regress, Grim Reaper, and Methuselah-style arguments, claims any one would suffice, and selects his novel dependence argument.

candidates.speaker: Graham Oppy
candidates.proposition: Merely asserting an argument's premises makes no epistemic progress beyond asserting its conclusion unless the premises receive an adequate status or defense.
candidates.attributionBasis: Loke explicitly invites Graham's comments, after which the new speaker frames his objection by contrasting atheistic assertion with premise assertion.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The objection challenges whether Loke's deductive presentation can establish its conclusion rather than simply relocating the disputed assertion.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Loke's presentation of a valid deductive route from its stated premises to a personal creator.

candidates.contextSummary: Oppy asks for the discussion's ground rules and argues that replacing a bare conclusion with disputed premises does not advance the case without explaining their epistemic standing.

candidates.speaker: Graham Oppy
candidates.proposition: Successive supporting arguments threaten a regress of disputed premises, potentially ending with claims whose standing is no better than the original conclusion.
candidates.attributionBasis: This turn follows Loke's promise to supply subarguments, and the speaker directly challenges that proposal using a regress objection.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The move presses the methodological objection against Loke's planned premise defenses and asks what could provide a satisfactory stopping point.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Loke's proposal to defend the causal principle and impossibility of infinite regress through further subarguments.

candidates.contextSummary: Oppy argues that each subargument introduces new premises that may also be rejected, producing a looming regress unless some premises become genuinely irresistible.

candidates.speaker: Graham Oppy
candidates.proposition: Theory is prior to argument because a person's accepted theory determines which premises and arguments they regard as true or sound.
candidates.attributionBasis: The sustained turn is Oppy's continuation of his ground-rules challenge and presents his explicit theory-first account of argumentative assessment.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This supplies Oppy's overarching framework for resisting premise-by-premise proof and reframes the debate as comparison of whole theories.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Loke's proposed method of establishing premises by offering reasons and rebutting alternative possibilities.

candidates.contextSummary: Oppy says theories determine attitudes toward premises; arguments chiefly expose inconsistency or uncomfortable consequences, while abstract soundness is not the proper primary focus.

candidates.speaker: Graham Oppy
candidates.proposition: Causation is fundamentally a relation between events, while talk of things as causes is a legitimate but derivative description.
candidates.attributionBasis: Oppy initiates the examination of the first premise and explicitly marks his Davidson-influenced account as his own preferred understanding.
candidates.loadBearingReason: Clarifying the relata of causation is necessary for evaluating Loke's series, his treatment of changes, and the proposed first cause.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Loke's first premise asserting a series of causes, effects, and changes without yet fixing the causal relata.

candidates.contextSummary: Oppy contrasts event and thing causation, explains their interdefinability through changing properties, and states that event causation is more fundamental though thing causation remains acceptable.

candidates.speaker: Graham Oppy
candidates.proposition: The shared premise that causal reality exists remains contestable because agreement between the debaters does not answer causal skeptics.
candidates.attributionBasis: Oppy explicitly distinguishes the two participants' agreement from the position of outside causal skeptics and comments on the premise's status.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The observation limits what the agreed first premise establishes and identifies an undefended assumption at the foundation of Loke's argument.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: The jointly accepted first premise that there is a causal network of items related as causes and effects.

candidates.contextSummary: Oppy accepts causal reality for the discussion but notes that skeptics reject it and that the participants have offered nothing here to persuade them.
